description: 102 distinct rāga entries (6 legacy duplicates from v2.1 merged) with Melakarta scale structure and traditional (Ayurvedic-style) associations. ayurvedic_srd_framework.title: The Svara–Rasa–Doṣa (SRD) Classical Music Therapy System
ayurvedic_srd_framework.conceptual_summary: In classical Ayurveda and Natyashastra, music therapy operates by using musical notes (Swaras) and melodic modes (Ragas) to evoke specific aesthetic relishes (Rasas), which modulate the subtle mental qualities (Trigunas: Sattva, Rajas, Tamas) to restore balance among the physical humors (Tridoshas: Vata, Pitta, Kapha). (Interpretive framework, not an evidence-based clinical protocol.)

vata.name: Vāta (Air & Ether)
vata.imbalance_manifestations: Anxiety, insomnia, restlessness, tremors, pain, mental wandering
vata.therapeutic_principle: Pacified by Karuṇā (pathetic/grounding), Śānta (tranquil), and Adbhuta (wondrous) rasas using Sāttvic-Tāmasic or pure Sāttvic modes.

pitta.name: Pitta (Fire & Water)
pitta.imbalance_manifestations: Anger, hyperpyrexia (fever), inflammation, hypertension, acid peptic disorders
pitta.therapeutic_principle: Pacified by Karuṇā (Sāttvic-Tāmasic cooling), Śānta (tranquil), and Adbhuta (wondrous) rasas; Ga and Ni predominant modes.

kapha.name: Kapha (Water & Earth)
kapha.imbalance_manifestations: Lethargy, depression, congestion, mental fog, emotional stasis
kapha.therapeutic_principle: Counteracted by Śrīṅgāra (erotic/vital) and Vīra (heroic) rasas possessing Sāttvic-Rājasic energy to stimulate movement and dynamism.

trigunas.sattva: Light, clarity, harmony, emotional balance — the primary target of psychological healing (Sattvāvajaya).
trigunas.rajas: Activity, passion, restlessness — mental disturbance causing agitation when in excess.
trigunas.tamas: Inertia, darkness, ignorance — mental disturbance causing depression and lethargy when in excess.

ayurvedic_srd_framework.framework_status: The Svara–Rasa–Doṣa (SRD) system is this project's own synthesis. The svara→rasa pairings in rows 1–4 follow the Nāṭyaśāstra tradition as reported in secondary literature; the guṇa and doṣa columns, and the Śānta row, are interpretive and have no classical svara-level source. No peer-reviewed clinical study validates the doṣa mapping.

sanskrit_textual_sources.text_name: Caraka Saṁhitā (c. 2nd Century BCE - 4th Century CE)
sanskrit_textual_sources.key_prescriptions: Reviewed in Prasad, J.S.R. (2022), "Therapeutic elements of music in ancient India: a brief review in Bṛhattrayī", doi:10.1007/s43539-022-00043-3: music is mentioned for Pitta aggravation, labour room, virility, tuberculosis, alcohol intoxication, and for a patient who has regained consciousness after coma, and a musician staff is listed in the hospital set-up. Verse numbers previously given (Vimānasthāna 6.17; Cikitsāsthāna 2/3.29-30, 8.186-188, 24.192-193; Sūtrasthāna 24.51-53, 15.7) were not independently checked.

sanskrit_textual_sources.text_name: Suśruta Saṁhitā (c. 6th Century BCE - 5th Century CE)
sanskrit_textual_sources.key_prescriptions: Per Prasad, J.S.R. (2022), "Therapeutic elements of music in ancient India: a brief review in Bṛhattrayī", doi:10.1007/s43539-022-00043-3: Suśruta prescribes music to rouse a patient from coma and for fainting during therapeutic emesis/purgation. Verses cited earlier (Uttaratantra 46.22-23; Cikitsāsthāna 34.12-13) were not independently checked. Note the contrast: Suśruta uses music to break a coma, whereas Caraka uses it after consciousness returns.

sanskrit_textual_sources.text_name: Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya & Aṣṭāṅga Saṅgraha by Vāgbhaṭa (c. 6th Century CE)
sanskrit_textual_sources.key_prescriptions: Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya Sūtrasthāna 13.6 is reported to say that Pitta disorders can be eased by pleasant music (Molligoda & Somarathna 2013). The Aṣṭāṅga Saṅgraha verse 'vallakīmadhuraṁ gītaṁ…' for burning fever was not independently checked.
Prenatal/perinatal music and post-meal music are attributed to Kāśyapa Saṁhitā; verse numbers (Khilasthāna 5.55-56) and the 7th-9th century dating (debated) were not independently checked.
Listed for completeness. No specific music-therapy passage was verified; the earlier line ('reaffirmation of receptive music therapy') was vague and has not been confirmed.

sanskrit_textual_sources.text_name: Nāṭyaśāstra (c. 2nd century BCE–2nd century CE) & Saṅgītaratnākara (13th century)
sanskrit_textual_sources.key_prescriptions: Nāṭyaśāstra defines eight rasas (Śānta was added later) and associates certain svaras with rasas (see svara_rasa_dosa_mapping). The 15 gamakas are listed in Śārṅgadeva's Saṅgītaratnākara, not the Nāṭyaśāstra. The previous 'NS 29.11' verse reference was not verified.

sanskrit_textual_sources.text_name: Saṅgīt Cikitsā by Dr. Pal (1938, Lahore)
sanskrit_textual_sources.key_prescriptions: Catalogued by Sangeet Natak Akademi (indianculture.gov.in). Describes the use of ragas for various illnesses with case studies. These are early-20th-century clinical observations, not controlled trials.
Prasad, J.S.R. (2022), "Therapeutic elements of music in ancient India: a brief review in Bṛhattrayī", doi:10.1007/s43539-022-00043-3. Used here as the check on Bṛhattrayī music references.

sanskrit_textual_sources.text_name: Randomized controlled trial: Kunikullaya et al. (2022), Eur J Investig Health Psychol Educ 12(10):108
sanskrit_textual_sources.key_prescriptions: 140 healthy young adults heard one session of Hindustani ragas Miyan ki Todi, Malkauns or Puriya, or natural sounds. State anxiety fell significantly with Puriya (p=0.018), followed by Malkauns and Miyan ki Todi. Single session, healthy participants, small groups; not evidence of treatment effect.

disclaimer: Cultural and educational content. Nothing here is medical advice, diagnosis or treatment, and no raga is a substitute for professional care. Raga-specific therapeutic effects have not been established by clinical research; entries describe scale structure and traditional associations only.

verification.summary: 72 Melakarta scales and names checked against the Melakarta table (formula + Wikipedia): all 72 scales were correct; 3 names and 1 spelling were fixed. Of the other 36 entries (12 early curated entries + 24 janyas): 9 have scale data verified against a source, 6 were corrected (parent, tradition label or scale), 3 remain unverified/flagged, and the rest are internally consistent with their stated parent only. Therapeutic text: 96 of the 108 entries carried identical generic template text and it was removed (preserved in legacy_template_text); the 12 hand-written entries were softened to traditional associations (originals preserved). The svara–rasa table keeps its four Nāṭyaśāstra rows; the Śānta row is flagged as having no classical basis. The condition index (106 of 108 rāgas under 'anxiety') was replaced.

limits: Janya scales marked consistent were checked only for internal agreement with the stated parent, not against a published lakshana.
The scanned book "A Historical Study of Indian Music" (Prajnanananda) could not be searched reliably (image-only PDF; OCR yielded little usable text) and was not used as a source.
The second uploaded PDF is a 2-page book review of Nagarajan (2021); it supports the framework at concept level (nāda, śruti, svara, rāga, rasa, jīva svara, doṣas) but contains no per-rāga data.
Citations such as "Raaga_and_Healing.pdf" are file names, not publications, and could not be checked.
sources: Bhavanani A.B. (2022) Book review: An Introduction to Indian Music Therapy, J Appl Conscious Stud 10:93-4 (uploaded PDF)

Converted all raga_id/ascii_id/canonical_raga_id values to plain ASCII; every former id is listed in "aliases" so old references still resolve.

Normalised "tradition" to "Carnatic" and kept the original wording in "tradition_original". Hindustani relationships are now explicit in "hindustani_counterpart" (same_pitch_set / different_scale / unconfirmed, with a source_checked flag).

Ghanta parent/scale conflict resolved from historical sources (bhāṣāṅga placement under Mela 20). Manji annotated with a source. Neelambari parent re-confirmed; its vakra scale string remains unverified.
Condition index: moved pain, hypertension, fever, digestive and respiratory lists to withheld_lists.

"consistent" janya scales were only checked for agreement with the stated parent.
